title: Latency‑aware answer stubs — playbook and rough PRD
content:
Overview:

This is a very rough personal playbook / PRD sketch for a feature I'm calling "Latency‑Aware Answer Stubs" (LAAS). Idea: when we detect likely or observed latency violations for a given request, the system can optionally return a concise, safe "stub" reply immediately (or near‑immediately) instead of waiting for a full expensive generation. The stub preserves conversational continuity, sets expectations, and allows the app to decide whether to request a full follow‑up generation asynchronously.

Why:
- Some product flows prioritize responsiveness over completeness (mobile UX, notifications, quick suggestions).
- Long tail p99/p999 token-generation spikes cost customers and cause perceived flakiness.
- Automatic graceful degradation reduces user churn while we surface degraded quality telemetry.

Primary goals (measurable):
- Reduce user‑visible time‑to‑first‑byte for prioritized routes by 30–60% in high‑latency incidents (experiment target).
- Provide a safe, consistent stub template so downstream apps have a predictable fallback contract.
- Enable asynchronous full result retrieval without losing context or creating confusing duplicate messages.
- Keep additional infra and cost minimal.

Non‑goals:
- Not intended to replace canned quick replies or system messages designed into the product UX.
- Not for use where correctness/complete output is mandatory (medical/legal). Those routes should opt‑out.

User stories (ordered by priority):
1) As a mobile user, when the model is slow, I get a quick short answer that is clearly labeled as a summary/stub; I can tap a "Get full answer" button to fetch a detailed reply.
2) As a developer, I can opt a route into LAAS via route config: {enable_stub: true, quality_tier: p95, max_stub_length: 40 tokens}.
3) As an ops engineer, I can see stub rate, stub success (did full answer arrive later), and stub->full quality delta in Console dashboards.
4) As a privacy officer, stub content must not contain protected info; stub generation must follow redaction rules and reuse any request‑level denylists.

Behavioral sketch / API semantics:
- Route config fields: enable_stub (bool), latency_threshold_ms (int), stub_policy (enum: auto|always|never), max_stub_tokens (int), label_text (string, optional).
- Simple semantics: when request enters runtime, an early latency estimate is computed (see Estimation below). If estimate > latency_threshold_ms and stub_policy != never, runtime races stub path vs full path: either return stub immediately (fast path) or continue normal generation.
- Stub payload: {text, is_stub: true, stub_reason: "latency_estimated", stub_id} Where stub_id allows correlation with follow‑up.
- Follow‑up: client can call GET /v1/responses/{stub_id}/full (or Webhook) to fetch full result once ready. Alternatively server can push full result asynchronously to the customer endpoint (configurable).

Stub generation strategies (options to explore):
A) Deterministic template: always return a short template like "Quick summary: [truncated placeholder]. Tap for full answer." (lowest risk).
B) Model‑synthesized stub: run a tiny constrained model (quantized 1–2 layer proxy or small Llama‑like) to produce a concise summary. (better UX, higher cost/complexity).
C) Extractive summarization from partial tokens/KV cache: if runtime has partial context or prefix cached we can synthesize a short answer from that state.

Tradeoffs:
- (A) is safest for compliance and easy auditability but less useful.
- (B) yields better perceived quality but means an extra model footprint and more complexity in routing and evaluation.
- (C) is technically elegant but increases coupling between runtime internals and API semantics.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Configurable per‑route opt‑in stub behavior in the console/API.
- Stubs returned for >= 5% of high‑latency sample traffic in experiment runs, with labeling is_stub=true.
- Full answer retrieval mechanism implemented (poll endpoint and webhook options).
- Console: stub_rate, stub_latency, percent_stub_followed_by_full, p95_full_latency while stubbing.
- Safety: stubs automatically strip PHI-like tokens and are blocked for routes with enforce_policy=high.

Metrics to measure:
- Stub rate (requests that returned a stub)
- Stub->Full conversion (client asked for full) and time to full
- Customer‑visible p95 / p99 latency improvements
- Delta in downstream satisfaction (NPS-like or A/B quality evals)
- Server cost overhead (extra small model or additional requests)
- Safety regression signals (redacted tokens leakage, PII incidents)

Quick rollout plan / experiment design:
- Phase 0: internal dogfood on Redwood Console workflows. Conservative templated stubs. Test on 2 internal routes. 2 week pilot. Manual monitoring.
- Phase 1: External beta for a handful of customers (product‑opted). Allow webhooks for full deliveries. Collect metrics and qualitative feedback.
- Phase 2: opt-in in hosted tiers; SDK support for client UI helper (client shows "Loading summary (tap to load full)").

Runtime/implementation notes (brain dump):
- Latency estimator: simple heuristic using model_type, requested max_tokens, current queue depth, slot_throughput; start with a linear predictor trained from historical traces (cheap).
- Placement: implement in gateway layer before heavy scheduling decisions to avoid occupying GPU slots for stubs.
- If we choose strategy (B), we need a tiny proxy model pool (CPU/GPU) with ultra‑fast cold/warm start. Consider quantized CPU inference (ONNX/ggml) or tiny GPU instance pool.
- Correlation id: add stub_id that maps to original request id + small hash. Keep TTL on stored partial/full results (e.g., 24h).
- Billing: stub responses billed at a reduced rate or 0? Need pricing discussion (product).

Safety & Compliance:
- Default: any route with compliance flag (hipaa/sox) -> stubbing disabled.
- Stub templates should not echo user PII; we should run the normal redaction checks (same as full path) on the stub text.

Open questions / TODOs (my priority):
- Q1: Should stubs be produced synchronously by same runtime (fast truncated generation) or by a separate microservice? Pros/cons.
- Q2: What is the minimal acceptable stub quality for customers? (Run a short user research session).
- Q3: Pricing model — likely an attribution charge for full; stubs probably free or nominal. Discuss with Finance.
- Q4: Mobile SDK changes: recommended client patterns (optimistic UI, polling vs push). Provide sample code snippets.
- Q5: What telemetry must be included to make rollback safe? (latency, stub_count, quality_eval).

Notes to self / ideas I want to try quickly:
- Quick prototype: gateway returns static template with context‑based one‑liner: "Short answer: {first 20 chars of model prefix}" as a stopgap so we can test UX without small model pool.
- Create a lightweight A/B: route A = no stub, route B = templated stub; capture conversion to full and downstream satisfaction.
- Add a flag in Sandbox to manually mark a request as "forced_stubbing" for debugging.

Potential failure modes & mitigations:
- Bad UX: users think stub is the real answer -> label clearly and provide CTA for full.
- Double costs: returning stub + full can double bill. Consider free stub or billing credit.
- Inconsistent semantics across deployments (Hosted vs Private) — document differences. Private deployments might want to disable small model pool; default to templated stubs there.

Related tickets / quick links (for later):
- JIRA-MLINF-462 (experiment infra)
- GH PR 87 (proposal doc)
- Confluence latency playbook link (above)

Last thoughts: keep MVP simple and conservative. Users are sensitive to trust; a clearly labeled stub that helps reduce latency likely wins more than an unlabelled low‑quality model answer. Next action: sync with Maya + Evan for feasibility and with Product PM to decide billing defaults.

-- Connor
